summary: Proposes a way around the race condition in the Initial Connection Protocol described in RFC 143. The Host-Host protocol did not say what to do with several requests to the same socket, so implementations differ. The suggestion is to fix it in a third-level protocol rather than change the Host-Host protocol.

eli5.summary: Two friends keep trying to call each other at the same instant. Instead of changing the phone system, the note changes how they start the call.

subtitle: How to avoid conflicting connection requests without changing the Host-Host protocol.

tldr.problem: The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) did not specify what to do when multiple connection requests arrived at the same socket simultaneously, causing different host implementations to behave differently.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of modifying the Host-Host protocol, use separate sockets for the connection initialization messages, so each request gets its own path.
tldr.outcome: This allows ICP to work correctly across implementations without requiring protocol changes, solving the race condition at a higher protocol layer.

today: RFC 161 is a historical record of an early protocol design issue. The ICP was later superseded by the TCP/IP suite, which handles connection establishment differently through the TCP three-way handshake.

sections.title: The Race Condition Problem
sections.content:
RFC 161 describes a problem in the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) for establishing connections between network hosts. When the Host-Host protocol received more than one request to the same socket, there was no rule saying what should happen. Some implementations (like SDC's) would queue the requests, while others (like UCLA's) would refuse the new request.

This led to incompatible behavior across the network. Since implementations differed fundamentally on how to handle this conflict, every pair of hosts had to negotiate their behavior.
sections.eli5: When two computers both tried to start a connection to the same place at the same time, some computers would wait in line and some would say 'no.' This made it hard for computers to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Solution: Separate Sockets
sections.content:
Rather than change the Host-Host protocol itself, Ari Shoshani proposed using a different socket for each direction of the connection initialization. When the server and user exchange their INIT messages, they would use sockets U+2 and U+3 instead of reusing the main connection socket.

This ensures that no two INIT messages target the same socket, so the race condition cannot occur. The solution is transparent to the Host-Host protocol and does not depend on any particular implementation's handling of simultaneous requests.
sections.eli5: Use different mailboxes for the start-of-call messages. If the server uses mailbox U+3 and the user uses mailbox U+2, they cannot collide.

sections.title: Why This Works
sections.content:
The solution proposed in RFC 143 to this same problem required that the NCP (network control program) could notify a process when a command arrived. This was implementation-dependent and not guaranteed.

Shoshani's approach avoids any assumptions about NCP notification. By using separate sockets from the start, the handshake completes without ever triggering the race condition, making it portable across any Host-Host implementation.
sections.eli5: This fix does not need the network to tell anyone anything special. It just uses different paths so there is no race at all.

references.text: Shoshani, A., "A Solution to the Race Condition in the ICP", RFC 161, May 1971.
